rows.en: Those who expounded the prophecies of the book took the parable for the thing it stood for, and there came out a picture of the Messiah that the prophets had not imagined: they thought that the Messiah is a son of man who will be revealed from among the clouds, as in the parable of the book, and they gave him a nature close to the divine. Fourth Ezra (ch. 13), in his visions, invents visions whose source, as all who see them will recognize, is the prophecies of Daniel; but he erred in their sense and took the parable for the thing signified, and the Messiah appeared to him as a heavenly being whom God had hidden for a long time (13:26), and he calls him son of God (ibid. 32). And the Book of Enoch (ch. 48 and in many places) calls him son of man, as in Daniel's parable, who sits in heaven and was named by name before the Ancient of Days, and who existed before the creation of the world. And although there is clear evidence that the hands of other editors have touched these two books, it is nevertheless clear that the mistaken sense given to the book of Daniel gave birth to all the strange views in the beliefs about the Messiah, all that is written in the two books mentioned; and these were planted among the Jews, and many even of the sages, early and late, could not part from them. They believed that the name of the Messiah was created before the world was created (Pesaḥim 54a), and that he is hidden and concealed because of the sins of Israel (Targum Jonathan Micah 4:8); and in the opinion of many he will be from the dead, and David himself will be the Messiah (Yerushalmi Berakhot ch. 2; Sanhedrin 98b); and he will be revealed and concealed and revealed again, and whoever believes in him will live, and whoever does not believe goes over to the nations of the world and is killed by them (Midrash Song of Songs and Ruth); and he suffers in every generation according to the sins of the generation (Pesikta Rabbati); the holy spirit will rest on him (Targum Jonathan Isaiah 42:2⚠1), and the radiance of holiness shines from the radiance of his face (ibid. 53:2); he will pray for mercy on Israel and by his merit their sins will be atoned, and he will deliver the wicked to Gehinnom (ibid. 53:4, 19⚠2); and he will build the Temple that was profaned through sins (ibid. 5), not by human hands but by the hands of Heaven (Mekhilta Shirah ch. 10; Ketubbot 5a; Ezra 13:36); and he will be sharp toward the nations (Sifre Deuteronomy piska 1), and will accuse them before the Holy One, blessed be He, and will judge them and Samael (Pesikta Rabbati; Ezra ibid.; Enoch ch. 54); but he is gentle toward Israel (Sifre ibid.), and will gather the dispersed, even the Ten Tribes, who were exiled beyond the Sambatyon (Ezra 13:40; Sanhedrin ch. 11), and the waters of the Euphrates will be cut off so that they can return (Ezra ibid. 47); and for those sunk in Riblah the Holy One, blessed be He, makes tunnels, and they go as far as the Mount of Olives, and it splits and they come up out of it (Pesikta Rabbati; and see Yerushalmi Sanhedrin end of ch. 10). And not only his nature and his deeds, but also the name of the Messiah they expounded (Sanhedrin 98b and in many places). Such expounding was already customary among the ancients. And the name Bar Kokhba was perhaps also a title for the Messiah, because they took the Torah's saying "there shall step forth a star out of Jacob" [Numbers 24:17] as a hint at the Messiah (see above, ch. 3); and there is found in the Gospel a story that wise men of the East came to Jerusalem to bow down before their Messiah because they had seen his star in the east, and this shows that a star was a figure for the Messiah at that time. And perhaps for this reason he was called in Babylonia Bar Nafle (Sanhedrin 96b), for nafle in Aramaic is a term for a star (R. Naḥum Brüll in the journal *Beit ha-Midrash*, 148). The pen cannot write all the inventions that the imagination devised to portray the Messiah and the conditions of his coming and his office (Pesikta Rabbati piska 35, 36 and in many places), mixing together husk and kernel, the possible and the impossible. Let us not think that these are late inventions, for their roots agree with the pictures of the books of Ezra and Enoch, which were composed in the days of the Temple. But although these views found believers among the common people and among some of the sages, they were nevertheless not principles of faith; they were only secondary pictures and offspring of aggadic midrashim, according to what they understood, or rather distorted, in the Scriptures, putting into them things that the prophets never thought of and that never came into their minds. Such expositions were like the degenerate shoots of the vine [Jeremiah 2:21] in the vineyard of Israel; they were not the views of the nation as a whole nor agreed beliefs. And just as even in our time, which is a time of enlightenment, there are still simpletons who believe every word [Proverbs 14:15], and yet we do not say on that account that their foolishness is the general, ruling belief, so it was in those days: even if many abounded in the children of vanity in the matter of the pictures of the Messiah, we do not say that their vanities were the general belief; for the enlightened did not abound in these, and their belief in the Messiah was pure of dross, and in the essence of the matter they did not stray far from the prophecies of the prophets and from the words of the sages down to their time. Now the principal beliefs were these: that close to the revelation of the Messiah troubles come, which are called the birth pangs of the Messiah (Shabbat 118a and in many places); and it would be, for example: "In the footsteps of the Messiah insolence will increase" (Sotah 49b). The insolence will show especially in that the youth will behave insolently against the elder and the base against the honorable [Isaiah 3:5], the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, a man's enemies are the men of his own house [Micah 7:6], and the ways of morals are corrupted (ibid. and Sanhedrin 97a). The period of preparation is seven years. The first three are evil and full of distress, and the Torah is forgotten by those who study it. In the fourth, plenty and not plenty; in the fifth, great plenty and joy, and the Torah returns to those who study it;{v1_12_13:1} in the sixth, voices; and in the seventh, wars (all this ibid.). And it is not the office of the Messiah to innovate anything in matters of religion (Eduyot 8:6⚠3), and the Torah is found with all Israel; they study it and do not forget it (Yalkut Exodus 273). After the years of preparation, the time has come for the kingdom of the nations to end and the time for the kingdom of Heaven to be revealed (Midrash Song of Songs on "the fig tree"), and then the redeemer will come. Although they believed that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the redeemer, and that the redeemed are the redeemed of the Lord, not the redeemed of the King Messiah (Midrash Psalms 107), and they believed from of old that the gathering of the exiles and the redemption would be completed and after that the Messiah would be revealed (Megillah 17b; Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:4), in accordance with the sense of the words of the prophets, they nevertheless gave the redemption the name "the coming of the son of David," and the Messiah is called "redeemer," whom God brings (the Eighteen Benedictions). This redeemer will be of the root of David, and his birthplace is Bethlehem of Judah (Targum Jonathan Micah 5; Yerushalmi Berakhot ch. 2); his office is to lead people to repentance toward the Lord (Song of Songs Rabbah on "your neck"), for the redemption depends on repentance (Sanhedrin 97b). He will bring many back to the Torah and pray for the sins of Israel (Targum Jonathan Isaiah 53:11), and the good God will forgive (ibid. 5); all idolatry will be uprooted, and the Lord will be alone in the world and His kingdom forever and ever (Mekhilta de-Amalek ch. 1); and this kingdom is guided by the Messiah, and there is no end to all the material and moral good, according to all the promises of the prophets (Targum Jonathan Isaiah 11, and in the Gemara and the midrashim in many places). These refined beliefs found their place in ancient prayers. Whoever considers the Eighteen Benedictions, to know what they asked for, will also understand what their hope was and recognize their picture of the redemption. Therefore, if we see in them that all their request was the attainment of understanding, repentance, purification from sin, deliverance from trouble, temporal good, the gathering of the exiles, the restoration of their political state, the subduing of the wicked, the destruction of wickedness from the earth, the reward of the righteous, the raising of the horn of Jerusalem, and the restoration of the kingdom of the house of David — is not the picture of the things that are fit to found and establish the happiness of the nation laid down in this request? From this we can judge the general belief, clean of any admixture of strange views. But the nature of the Messiah and all the particular secondary pictures were for them among the things hidden from human beings (Mekhilta Va-yassa ch. 4 and 5; Pesaḥim 54b).

rows.en: Just as the enlightened thought it wrong to expound on the "how," so they thought it wrong to expound on the "when"; for the end, the time of the Messiah's revelation, was also among the things hidden from human beings (Mekhilta and Gemara ibid.). But if, all the same, at the end of the days of the Temple the calculation of the end was a matter with which the sages occupied themselves, they did this only to revive the heart of the crushed and to give them hope that salvation was near to come. The prophecy in the book of Daniel they interpreted as referring to their own time, and they expounded the saying "a time, times, and half a time" [Daniel 7:25] as referring to the last period of the days of the Temple (Sanhedrin 97a, and Rashi there). But for the honor of the sages of the Oral Torah we will say that they intended only to strengthen the hope of the people and rested their consolations on the words of the book; it is impossible that they thought that this was the meaning of the book, for whoever considers it with a settled mind will see that the book speaks of the end of the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes. Now this calculation proved false. The time passed, the calculation ran out, and the hoped-for Messiah did not come; instead came double trouble. Yet the gates of hope were not locked. They quickly found a new opening: R. Akiva came in his time, expounded the Scriptures and made a calculation suited to his time (97 ibid.). And as the troubles multiplied, so the calculations multiplied, and none of them proved true, until the later sages returned to the principal belief: that the end is hidden from the eye of every living thing, and the Lord knows. And they saw reason to hold to this with even greater force, since they saw that many calculators of the end, when they saw that their calculation did not come to pass, despaired and said: "Since the end has arrived and he has not come, he will no longer come." Therefore all people of settled mind loathed it⚠1 and took upon themselves not to make calculations, for the Messiah comes only when the mind is diverted (ibid. 97a). Likewise there was no agreed belief about the measure of the time of the days of the Messiah; there were various views on this, all of them results of their midrash or children of the imagination (Sanhedrin 99a and in many places, and in the books of Ezra and Enoch). And now we see that the belief in the redemption shared by the whole nation was only in the principal foundations and not in the secondary matters. R. Akiva saw that Bar Kokhba was doing valiantly against the Roman legions; therefore he held him to be the Messiah. And have we heard that he examined whether the secondary matters that were ascribed to the Messiah were fulfilled in him? Everyone knows that he was like any other man: he did not come down from heaven and did not trace his descent to the house of David; and nevertheless R. Akiva and his generation held him to be the Messiah. Some time later a sage of the Pharisees named R. Hillel arose and said: "There is no Messiah for Israel" (Sanhedrin 98b). He certainly did not deny the redemption. Perhaps he even admitted that when it is the will of the Lord to redeem Israel, the hand of one of the men of high rank will be in the midst, who with the help of God will work salvation for His people; but he denied the secondary attributes that were attached to the time of redemption, together with a human redeemer who stands above nature, and this is what he meant in saying "There is no Messiah for Israel." And one of the sages of the aggadah said that those who return in the gathering of the exiles will be the redeemed of the Lord, not the redeemed of Elijah nor the redeemed of the King Messiah (Midrash Psalms 107); from this saying too the idea flashes forth not to ascribe the redemption to the Messiah: rather God will redeem His people and raise up His kingdom, and it is the kingdom of Heaven, and in this kingdom a king will reign, and he is called the King Messiah. And one of the sages of the Talmud said: "There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah except subjugation to the kingdoms alone" (Berakhot 34b). How could he say so if he had believed in all the strange inventions that were attached to the King Messiah and to his kingdom? Indeed, from the time when those secondary views became the work of man and harmed the faith of Israel, it was a need of the hour to teach the opposite and to strip from the belief in the Messiah the husk that the imagination had attached to it. And if the attributes that we consider the husk of the kernel had been a principle of their faith from ancient days, how would all these sages have dared to deny what their predecessors held as a principle of faith? But so it is: the principal foundations of the belief in the Messiah were shared by all, but in the secondary matters each one had his own teaching in his hand.

rows.en: After the kingdom of the Messiah is revealed there will be the resurrection of the dead. Both the righteous and the wicked will stand up at the resurrection, these to everlasting life and those to reproaches and everlasting abhorrence (Daniel 12:2; Sanhedrin 108a); and both Israel and the nations of the world have their share in the resurrection, except the generation of the Flood, the generation of the Dispersion and the people of Sodom (ibid. ch. 10), and their pious ones have a share in the world to come. The book of Ezra assigns to the nations of the world a terrible portion in the world of the resurrection (ch. 7). The resurrection comes together with the great day of judgment, when God will bring into judgment all the creatures of the worlds. The present world will pass away and wear out, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will create a new world (Sanhedrin 92b). These are the principal beliefs about the world of the resurrection and the day of judgment, which will come after the days of the Messiah; on them there was agreement among all the Pharisees, and they are compressed into short phrases: the day of Gog and Magog, the birth pangs of the Messiah, the day of consolation, the kingdom of the house of David, the days of the Messiah, the time to come, the resurrection of the dead, the depth of judgment, the great day, the world to come, the new world (Mekhilta Va-yassa ch. 4 and 5, and in the Gemara and the Midrash in many places). But these two principles too, the resurrection of the dead and the great day of judgment, were a matter with which the spirit of the expounders occupied itself in all generations; they devised devices in the Holy Scriptures to stand in the counsel of the Lord, and from every fine and small hint they drew out great and wonderful things and produced mountains hanging by a hair. The lofty idea of reward and punishment in the world to come was profaned by material pictures. There came forth the aggadah of the Leviathan whom the Lord killed and salted for the righteous in the time to come; of the beasts on a thousand hills [Psalms 50:10], which are also kept for the righteous (Bava Batra 74b); of the wine kept in its grapes since the six days of creation (Berakhot 34b); of the dew with which the Holy One, blessed be He, will revive the dead (Ḥagigah 12b; Yerushalmi Berakhot ch. 5); of the women who will give birth every day, and the trees that will bring forth fruit every day, and of the cakes and garments of fine wool that the Land of Israel will bring forth (Shabbat 30b); that the righteous will rise in their clothes (Ketubbot 111b); in what manner man will be formed in the world to come and which part of the body will be renewed first (Genesis Rabbah ch. 14); of the Jerusalem of the world to come (Bava Batra 75b and in many places); and hundreds of such aggadot, all of which were flying in the air at that time. And although most of them became known only from the mouths of the later sages, they were nevertheless ancient, and their counterparts are in the books of Fourth Ezra and Enoch; but they were not among the principles of their faith. Rather, the custom of expounding every slight hint in the Scriptures gave birth to them. We can only lament that these views did harm from the day of their birth through many generations to come, and darkened the pure beliefs in Israel. But so it was from of old and so it will be forever: the greater the worth and the preciousness of some man or thing, so much the more, in proportion, will various aggadot attach to it in the course of time. Therefore we will also not wonder when we see that the very principle of the belief in the resurrection of the dead became for the aggadah a beloved and dear matter to delight in. How great the worth of the belief in the resurrection of the dead was for them, we can estimate if we consider their great efforts to uphold and preserve it. Already in the days of the first Scribes they strove to make it known and enacted that it should have a mention in the text of the prayer. They also enacted that all who concluded benedictions in the Temple should say "from everlasting to everlasting" (Berakhot ch. 9), deliberately against those who denied this principle. For already the ancient Kutim [Samaritans] did not believe in the resurrection of the dead. After that came the Sadducees and denied it, casting doubt on the antiquity of the tradition and thinking that this view had not grown in the field of the religion of the Torah, but that they had brought it up with them from Babylonia, since among the Persians the belief in the resurrection of the dead was rooted. And they paid no attention to the proofs from Scripture that the Pharisees brought them (Sanhedrin 90b).{v1_12_16:1} The principle of the belief in the resurrection of the dead was almost of equal weight with the principle of the belief in Torah from Heaven, for of both they said that whoever denies them has no share in the world to come. These beliefs and views struck root in the vineyard of Israel and became a mighty tree that bore branches and made fruit [Ezekiel 17:23]; the Torah of Moses and the prophets was its soil, and by the springs of wisdom it sent out its roots; and the sages of every generation guarded it and raised it up, and it prospered, multiplying branches and lengthening its boughs. Time after time they grafted foreign shoots onto it, but through the wisdom of its keepers the foreign shoots changed their nature and became like all the boughs of the tree, resembling them in their beauty, until these and those alike were holy, and all who saw them recognized that they are the seed that the Lord has blessed [Isaiah 61:9]. For the wise of our nation, the heads of the people and its leaders, who were called to keep the way of the tree of life [Genesis 3:24], the Torah and the religion of Israel, were not grudging toward the views and the laws of other peoples; rather, whatever was right in their eyes and fit to add learning and moral instruction and to increase knowledge, they chose and brought near, and they accepted the truth from whoever said it; and the certainty of these words of truth [Proverbs 22:21] was holy to them as if its root were in their own soil, and they strove with all their might to show that these truths were founded in the Torah of the Jews and were given to them from their own. But when a man rose up from among them, or even sects, who devised devices to plant a stranger's slips [Isaiah 17:10] in the vineyard of their Torah, which had neither the fragrance of Lebanon nor the glory of Sinai — as indeed happened at various times — then they too stood firm for our people and gave their lives for their Torah, and with doubled strength the faithful keepers guarded their vineyard and were a shield for the Torah, and did not let it be corrupted or cease from its purity. And if many say to themselves: "See, the tree is dead, its stock is dead in the ground [Job 14:8]; is it not far better for us to exchange the stock of the tree and plant it a choice vine, a faithful planting, that will bud and blossom and bear fruit, whose glory will be greater than the first, and that will live forever?" — then they too will answer and say to them: "In vain do you murmur against the Torah of the living God, given as an everlasting statute, whose foundations will never be moved. See, this tree that you thought dead, its stock in the ground, is still alive and will live forever; it has not lost its strength and its scent is not changed [Jeremiah 48:11]; as on the day it was planted it flourishes and will not cease from yielding fruit [Jeremiah 17:8]; and as then, so now too it will bud and blossom and give its fruit for praise and for glory in the earth."
The relation of the Oral Torah to the books of the Gospels and their views

In almost every generation adversaries rose against Israel who sought to uproot the tree of its religion from its root. How many nations and kingdoms rose against them and thought to wipe out the name of Israel from the earth; how many sages and writers among the nations despised them, mocked them, and sought to profane the honor of their Torah and to make their faith and customs a derision among the peoples; within them too adversaries rose up, namely the religious tendencies: the Sadducees, the Essenes and all the parties of dispute within the Pharisees themselves. All these oppositions, born at home or born abroad [Leviticus 18:9], were a curse to the house of Israel; but the harm was only material, to the adherents of the religion, not moral, to the religion itself. For as its opponents multiplied, so the love of the Jews for it grew. Against the enmity from outside they girded themselves to stand for their lives, and against their opponents from within they set a guard; but we have not heard or seen that they went down against these or those to the point of life⚠1. The greatest denial in their eyes was that of one who denies Torah from Heaven or the resurrection of the dead, and even so they did not sentence such deniers to a temporal punishment but to an eternal one, and said of them that they have no share in the world to come. But at the end of the days of the Temple there arose one opposition that vexed them more than all before it: the opposition of the Messianic Jews. The adherents of the sect were persecuted, and with them also their master. The cause of this evil and bitter lot was not his new tendency in the religion of the Jews, but the foundations on which he built his tendency; and his sentence was not the fruit of his teaching but the fruit of the means and the instruments through which he chose to give his teaching existence. For if we consider his teaching we will find that it is not a new teaching, but all of it, from beginning to end, is the teaching of the Jews dressed in a new garment. With regard to the Oral Torah he followed the Sadducees and said that it is a human invention and a commandment of men learned by rote [Isaiah 29:13], by means of which the Pharisees uproot the commandments of the written Torah (Matthew 15); and in his deeds and customs he followed the Essenes. His relation to John the Essene and his disciples shows that he had an inclination to the teaching of the Essenes, and so it appears from the customs of his life and from the course of his thoughts and beliefs. Now the marks of the Essenes are the desire to attain prophecy and to heal the sick by skill in charms; wealth they did not seek, and they chose common property within their society and lived a life of hardship; and these are hinted at also in their writings, and all these are surely the marks of the Essenes. Nevertheless most of his teaching is the teaching of the Jews and also, for the most part, in agreement with the views of the Pharisees. Does he not testify of himself that he did not come to uproot the Torah of Moses and the prophets but to fulfill it (ibid. 5:17)? And the concept of this fulfillment is going beyond the measure of the Torah and adding stringencies to what the Torah made strict. This is clear from the particulars counted there, by which he describes the manner of the fulfillment; and in the language of the sages one would say of such fulfillment: making a fence for the Torah. Whoever considers the particulars of the fulfillment there will find that most of them are fences that the Pharisaic sages also set.{v1_12_17:1} So too his making the commandment of love a great principle in the Torah (ibid. 22:39–40), and "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow: that is the principal thing, and the rest is commentary" (ibid. 7:12), and acts of kindness to an enemy (ibid. 5:44): for all this there is a source in Holy Scripture and in the words of our sages, and it is engraved in the life of our nation and in all its ways in the world from the time it became a nation until this day.{v1_12_17:2} So too his principles on the merits⚠2 of the lowly, the crushed, the humble and those who thirst for righteousness, on the reward of the merciful, that they will obtain mercy, the pure in heart, that they will receive the presence of the Shekhinah, the lovers of peace, that they are called children of the Omnipresent, and those persecuted for their righteousness, that they will attain the kingdom of Heaven (ibid. 5:3–10): these are found literally, word for word, in Holy Scripture and in the words of our sages. And his principles on the love of God for His creatures, that He is good to all (ibid. 5:45),{v1_12_17:3} and on love for Him and cleaving to Him, to be merciful as He is merciful (Luke 6:36), to believe in His power and to trust in Him without worrying today about tomorrow's livelihood (Matthew 6:31–33); on the payment of reward measure for measure (ibid. 7:2); on doing good not in order to receive a reward (Luke 6:35); that those who do good in secret receive their reward openly (Matthew 6:4);{v1_12_18:1} and the principle of the repair of the world in the kingdom of Heaven, by the removal of sin and the spread of moral good, independent of anything political (in many places): all these are principles of the teaching of the Pharisees.{v1_12_18:2} And besides these principles listed, most of his sayings and parables are found in the books of the Jews, and especially in the books of the Oral Torah;{v1_12_18:3} and therefore it has become clear that most of his teaching is from the teaching of the Pharisees.

footnotes.en: The wording of the verse is: "And at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone that shall be found written in the book" [Daniel 12:1]; and the commentators explained that "everyone that shall be found" refers to "your people," that is, everyone of the people who is written in the book of life. In my opinion a kaf has dropped out of the word kol because two kafs stand next to each other in the words ʿammekha kol, and one should read ke-khol ha-nimtsa katuv ba-sefer, "according to all that is found written in the book"; and he meant by it the Aramaic part of the book of Daniel, which is a book by itself, and there the matter of the kingdom of the Messiah is set out.

This is the reading in the Gemara, but it seems to me that the version was: "and the Torah returns to its newness and is renewed for Israel," as it is in Midrash Song of Songs on "the fig tree"; and they corrected it in the Babylonian Talmud so as not to give an opponent room to say that the perfection of the Messiah will be a new Torah. Some scholars have already understood this saying in the Midrash in that direction; they are cited in the book *Foundations of the Beliefs of the Jews*⚠1 by De Wette⚠2, p. 176; but they did not understand the plain sense of the words. For this saying is directed against their statement that in the third year the Torah will be forgotten by those who study it; against this it says that in the fifth it will return to its newness, so that after the forgetting it will be as new. And it is always their way to describe love of the Torah by its being as new in the eyes of those who study it; see Sifre Va-etḥanan piska 33, and Berakhot 63b. But Jewish sages too inclined to this view, and it is said explicitly in Yalkut Isaiah remez 296 that the Holy One, blessed be He, sits (in the Garden of Eden) and expounds a new Torah that He will give through the Messiah; and without doubt the one who said that the commandments will be abolished in the time to come (Niddah 61b) meant this, and this refers to the time after the resurrection.

footnotes.en: Rabban Gamaliel brought the Sadducees a proof of the resurrection of the dead from the Torah, from the Prophets and from the Writings, and it is a wonder that he did not bring a proof from Daniel. Perhaps Rabban Gamaliel deliberately refused to bring a proof from a late writer like Daniel, because this was the very claim of the Sadducees, that the belief in the resurrection of the dead had been learned from the Persians; and therefore there is no proof from the late Writings.
